01.note: Rabbi Abbahu warns that a person should never impose excessive fear on his household, because a great man once did and his household fed him something carrying a grave prohibition. The Gemara names the man as Rabbi Ḥanina ben Gamliel, then objects that God would not let a righteous man eat forbidden food. So, the Gemara explains, they only tried to feed him a limb cut from a living animal: one day his meat was missing a limb, and his frightened household cut one from a live animal to make the meal look whole, and he almost ate it.
01.why: The discussion has just quoted Rav that a man who terrifies his household will end up in serious sins, and that household instructions on Shabbat eve must be given calmly. Rabbi Abbahu's account is a concrete case of that danger.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: The Sage who gives the warning and tells the story.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Gamliel
people.about: The 'great man' whose household feared him so much that they nearly fed him forbidden meat.

terms.meaning: Meat cut from an animal while it is still alive. Eating it is forbidden to all people, and the Gemara counts it a grave prohibition.

02.note: Mar Ukva, the Exilarch (head of the Jewish community) in Babylonia, wrote to Rabbi Elazar in the Land of Israel: people were tormenting him, and he had the power to hand them over to the government. May he? Rabbi Elazar answered with a verse about keeping a curb on one's mouth while the wicked stand before you. Mar Ukva wrote again that the torment was too much to bear. Rabbi Elazar answered: be silent before the Lord, and He will strike them down; go early and stay late at the study hall, and they will disappear on their own. Soon after, Geneiva, Mar Ukva's tormentor, was put in a neck iron by the government.
02.why: The Gemara has been talking about letters sent from the Land of Israel to Babylonia and the scoring of lines on parchment before writing a verse; Rabbi Elazar's replies are such letters. The next passages pick up the theme of staying silent and leaving judgment to God.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: The Exilarch in Babylonia, who is being tormented and asks whether he may hand his tormentors to the government.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage in the Land of Israel who answers Mar Ukva's letters with verses.

people.name: Geneiva
people.about: Mar Ukva's tormentor, who ends up in a neck iron.

terms.meaning: Drew faint guide lines on the parchment before writing. Writing verses from the Bible required this.
An iron collar put on a prisoner condemned by the government.

03.note: The Exilarch, head of the Babylonian Jewish community, asked Rav Huna where the ban on putting a garland on a bridegroom's head comes from. Rav Huna said it is a rabbinic rule, decreed during Vespasian's war. When Rav Huna stepped out to relieve himself, his student Rav Ḥisda, who had kept silent out of respect, offered a verse from Ezekiel: remove the mitre and take off the garland. He explained that once the High Priest's mitre was gone, the bridegroom's garland went too. Rav Huna came back, found them discussing it, and swore by God that the ban is only rabbinic, but praised Rav Ḥisda with a pun on his name: your name is Ḥisda and your words find favor.
03.why: The discussion has turned to the mourning customs after the Temple's destruction: Mar Ukva has just ruled that song is forbidden. The question of wedding garlands is another such custom, and the verse Rav Ḥisda finds is taken up again in what follows.

people.name: The Exilarch
people.about: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who asks the question.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage and Rav Ḥisda's teacher, who says the ban on garlands is rabbinic.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Rav Huna's student, who speaks up only once his teacher has left the room.

terms.meaning: A rule made by the Sages, as opposed to one written in the Torah itself.
The turban worn by the High Priest in the Temple.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses and quotes.

04.note: Ravina came upon Mar bar Rav Ashi braiding a garland for his daughter's wedding. Ravina asked him whether he did not hold by the verse 'Remove the mitre and take off the garland,' which had been read as banning wedding garlands. Mar bar Rav Ashi answered that the ban is modeled on the High Priest, so it applies to men only, not to women.
04.why: The Gemara has just derived the ban on bridegrooms' garlands from a verse about the High Priest's mitre. This incident marks the limit of that ban: it covers grooms, not brides.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who questions Mar bar Rav Ashi.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who is braiding a wedding garland for his daughter.

terms.meaning: The turban worn by the High Priest in the Temple.

05.note: Rav Huna and Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef were sitting before Rabbi Yirmeya, who was dozing. Rav Huna argued that if a third party seizes a debtor's property for a creditor, he acquires it for him. Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef asked: even when that hurts other creditors? Rav Huna said yes. Just then Rabbi Yirmeya woke up and said to them: 'Children! This is what Rabbi Yoḥanan said: one who seizes property for a creditor where it hurts others does not acquire it.' He explained that the mishna's case is different, because anyone who says 'give' is like one who says 'acquire.'
05.why: The mishna rules that a master cannot take back a bill of freeing a slave once he hands it to an agent. Rav Huna tried to draw a rule about debt collection from that; Rabbi Yirmeya shows why the mishna does not prove it. Rav Ḥisda then links the question to an older dispute.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who draws a conclusion about seizing property for a creditor.

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef
people.about: A Sage who presses Rav Huna with a follow-up question.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: The senior Sage they sit before; he dozes, then wakes and corrects them.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The Sage whose ruling Rabbi Yirmeya quotes.

terms.meaning: The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses. Here it is the ruling on bills freeing a slave.
To take legal ownership of something, here on behalf of someone else.

06.note: Some gardeners settled their accounts with each other, and one of them turned out to be holding five extra coins. The others told him, in front of the landowner, to give the money to the landowner, and the landowner made a formal act of acquisition with him. Later the gardener redid the sums himself and found he owed nothing. He came to Rav Naḥman, who said there was nothing he could do: a transfer made in the presence of all three parties is final, and the landowner had formally acquired the money besides. Rava objected that the gardener was not refusing to pay; he was saying the money was never owed. Rav Naḥman agreed: then it was an acquisition made in error, and any acquisition made in error is undone.
06.why: The Gemara has been discussing Rav's rule that a transfer made with all three parties present takes effect at once. Rav Naḥman applies that rule to this case, and Rava's objection shows where it stops: a transfer based on a mistake does not stand.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The Sage the gardener comes to with his case.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who points out that the gardener is disputing the debt, not refusing to pay it.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Quoted by Rav Naḥman as the source of Rav's rule on transfers.

terms.meaning: A coin; five of them is the sum in dispute.
A formal legal act that makes a transfer of property or an obligation binding.

07.note: Rav Sheshet was owed money for cloaks he had given merchants to sell in the city of Meḥoza. He asked Rav Yosef bar Ḥama to bring him the money on his way back. Rav Yosef collected it, and the merchants asked to make a formal act of acquisition with him, which would make him responsible for the money on the road. He said yes, but in the end he slipped away without doing it. When he told Rav Sheshet, Rav Sheshet said he had done well. In one version, because he had not made himself the 'borrower who is a slave to the lender'. In another, because the merchants, as the borrowers, should bear the risk until the money arrives.
07.why: The Gemara is discussing who bears the risk when money is sent through a messenger, and whether the sender can take it back. This incident shows a messenger avoiding that risk, and Rav Sheshet approving.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: A Sage owed money for cloaks sold in Meḥoza.

people.name: Rav Yosef bar Ḥama
people.about: The man Rav Sheshet sends to collect the money.

terms.meaning: A formal legal act that makes an obligation binding. Here it would have made Rav Yosef liable if the money were lost.

08.note: Rabbi Aḥai, son of Rabbi Yoshiya, had a silver vessel in the city of Neharde'a and asked Rabbi Dostai bar Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Yosei bar Keifar to bring it to him. The people holding it handed it over, then demanded that the two accept formal responsibility for it. When they refused, the people demanded the vessel back. Rabbi Dostai agreed; Rabbi Yosei refused, and the people tormented him. When he appealed to Rabbi Dostai, Rabbi Dostai told them, 'Well done, hit him.' Back home Rabbi Yosei complained to Rabbi Aḥai, who asked Rabbi Dostai why he had done this. Rabbi Dostai described the men: huge, with frightening names, ready to tie up or kill anyone on command. Had they killed him, who would give his father Yannai another son like him? Rabbi Aḥai's reply is not given here.
08.why: The Gemara is discussing who bears the risk when an item is sent through messengers, and whether the senders may retract. Just before, Rav Sheshet's messenger avoided taking on that risk; here two messengers refuse it and the senders try to take the vessel back.

people.name: Rabbi Aḥai
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yoshiya; owner of the silver vessel.

people.name: Rabbi Dostai bar Rabbi Yannai
people.about: One of the two messengers; he gives in to the men and tells them to hit his colleague.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei bar Keifar
people.about: The other messenger, who refuses to return the vessel and is tormented for it.

people.name: Yannai
people.about: Rabbi Dostai's father, named in his defense.

terms.meaning: A formal legal act; here it would have made the messengers responsible for the vessel on the way.

08.flag: The STORY segments end with Rabbi Dostai's defense; Rabbi Aḥai's verdict ('you acted well') is in the next segment, outside the span.

09.note: The Sages told Rabbi Elazar of an incident: the mother of the sons of Rokhel, when ill, said, 'Give my brooch to my daughter.' The brooch was worth twelve hundred dinars. She died, and the Sages carried out her words. Rabbi Elazar answered with a curse: 'May their mother bury the sons of Rokhel.' The Gemara explains he meant that no proof can be drawn from that case: the sons were wicked, so the Sages let their sister have the jewel.
09.why: The Gemara is explaining a dispute about a dying person who sends money with the word 'deliver.' It ties that to a mishna in which Rabbi Elazar says a dying person's gift needs a formal act, and the Rabbis say words alone suffice. The Rabbis bring this incident as proof; Rabbi Elazar rejects it.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage who holds that even a dying person's gift needs a formal act of acquisition.

people.name: The mother of the sons of Rokhel
people.about: An ill woman who left her brooch to her daughter by word alone, then died.

terms.meaning: A silver coin; twelve hundred of them made the brooch a very valuable piece.

10.note: Rabba bar bar Ḥana was ill, and Rav Yehuda and Rabba went to visit him. While there they asked him a legal question: must two people who bring a bill of divorce from overseas declare that it was written and signed in their presence? He said no, since if they testified that the divorce happened in their presence they would be believed anyway. Meanwhile a Persian priest came in and took the lamp away from them. Rabba said: 'Merciful One! Let us live either in Your shadow or in the shadow of the descendants of Esau,' meaning the Romans.
10.why: The discussion is about two messengers bringing a bill of divorce from abroad; Rabba bar bar Ḥana's answer bears on that. The lamp episode leads the Gemara to ask whether living under Rome is really better than under Persia.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Ḥana
people.about: The sick Sage who is visited and answers the question.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: One of the two Sages who visit him.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: The other visitor, who cries out after the lamp is taken.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.
A Zoroastrian priest. On a Persian festival, the translation explains, no one was allowed to keep a light burning outside their temple.

11.note: A man told ten men, 'Write a bill of divorce for my wife.' Two of them signed it that day, and the rest signed over the next ten days. He came to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi to ask whether it was valid. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said that Rabbi Shimon, who allowed a bill of divorce written by day and signed at night, is worthy of being relied on in a pressing situation, so the divorce stands.
11.why: The Gemara has just set out how Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish differ when a husband asks ten men to sign, including the case of two signing on the day and the rest later. This ruling is that very case, and the Gemara goes on to ask whose view it follows.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: The Sage who rules on the case.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: An earlier Sage whose lenient view Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi relies on.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end a marriage. It must be signed by witnesses.

12.note: A certain man let witnesses who could not sign their names trace them over a stencil on documents other than a bill of divorce. Rav Kahana had him flogged for it.
12.why: The Gemara has just said that letting witnesses trace their names is allowed only for bills of divorce, so that a woman is not left unable to remarry, and not for financial documents. This case shows that limit enforced.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: The Sage who orders the man flogged.

terms.meaning: Whipped; here a punishment given by the court for breaking a rule of the Sages.

13.note: A man threw what he said was a bill of divorce to his wife, among the barrels in her courtyard. Later all that was found there was a mezuza. Rav Naḥman ruled that a mezuza is rarely found among barrels, so it must be what the man threw, and not a bill of divorce.
13.why: The Gemara is asking when a document handed to a wife can be trusted as a bill of divorce, and when the husband can later say it was something else. Here the object itself is in doubt.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The Sage who rules on the case.

terms.meaning: A small parchment scroll with verses from the Torah, fixed to a doorpost.
The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.

14.note: A man went into the synagogue, took a Torah scroll, gave it to his wife and said, 'This is your bill of divorce.' Rav Yosef asked why there should be any concern. If the worry is that he had written a bill of divorce on it in gall water that has since faded, gall water does not hold on parchment that was itself prepared with gall water.
14.why: The discussion just before deals with doubtful bills of divorce, and with gall water as a writing liquid. The Gemara goes on to say that Rav Yosef's real point is that rule: gall water does not stay on parchment prepared with gall water.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who rules that there is nothing to be concerned about.

terms.meaning: Water in which gallnuts were soaked, used as a writing liquid and to prepare parchment.
The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.

15.note: A bill of divorce turned up at Rav Huna's court. It named the place as 'Sheviri, the city on the Rakhis River,' and Rav Huna worried there might be two towns called Sheviri, so it might belong to a different couple. Rav Ḥisda told Rabba, then a student, to go and look into it, because Rav Huna would ask him about it that night. Rabba went, examined it, and found a mishna: all documents issued by a court are returned to their owner.
15.why: The Gemara is asking when a lost bill of divorce may be returned. It uses this incident to resolve an apparent contradiction between two rulings of Rabba: the worry about a second person with the same name counts only where two such people are known to exist.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage whose court the bill of divorce is brought to.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: A Sage who sends Rabba to look into the question.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: At this time a student; he finds the source that settles it.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses and quotes.

16.note: Rabba bar bar Ḥana lost a bill of divorce he was delivering, in the study hall. He said that if they asked for a distinguishing mark he had one, and if they relied on recognition by sight he could recognize it. They returned it to him. Afterward he said he did not know which was the reason: the distinguishing mark, meaning they held such marks count by Torah law, or his recognition, which is trusted only from a Torah scholar and not from an ordinary person.
16.why: The Gemara has just said that Rav Ashi was unsure whether returning a lost item by its distinguishing marks is Torah law or a rule of the Sages. Rabba bar bar Ḥana's case leaves the same question open.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Ḥana
people.about: A Sage who loses a bill of divorce he was delivering and gets it back.

terms.meaning: A specific detail of a lost item, such as a hole next to a certain letter, that proves who owns it.
Knowing an item simply by sight, without naming a specific mark.
A rule from the Torah itself, as opposed to one the Sages added.

17.note: A man sent a bill of divorce to his wife with a messenger, who said he did not know her. The husband told him to give it to Abba bar Minyumi, who knew her, and he would deliver it. The messenger could not find Abba bar Minyumi, but he found Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa and Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa, with Rav Safra sitting among them. The three told him to hand his task over to them, and they would pass it to Abba bar Minyumi. Rav Safra objected that this messenger had never been given the power to carry out the divorce, so he could not pass it on. The three Sages were embarrassed.
17.why: The discussion just before is about when a messenger delivering a bill of divorce may appoint another in his place. Rava and Rav Ashi then argue over whether Rav Safra's objection was right.

people.name: Abba bar Minyumi
people.about: The man the husband trusted to recognize his wife and deliver the bill of divorce.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: One of three Sages who offer to take over the messenger's task.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina bar Pappa
people.about: One of the three Sages.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa
people.about: One of the three Sages.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: A Sage sitting with them who objects to their ruling.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.
A messenger appointed to act on someone's behalf, here to hand over a bill of divorce.

18.note: A man sent a bill of divorce to his wife with a messenger and told him not to deliver it for thirty days. Within the thirty days something beyond the messenger's control kept him from waiting. He came to Rava, who compared him to a messenger who falls ill and may appoint another, and told him to hand his task to the court, which would appoint a new messenger after thirty days. The Sages objected that he had no power to divorce yet; Rava answered that since he would have it after thirty days, he counts as having it. They objected again: perhaps the husband would make up with his wife in the meantime, and they cited a ruling to prove the concern. Rava was embarrassed. In the end it came out that the woman was only betrothed, and Rava said that worry does not apply to a betrothed woman.
18.why: Just before, Rav Safra ruled that a messenger never given the power to divorce cannot pass his task on. This case tests that rule on a messenger whose power only starts after thirty days. The Gemara then asks whether the court must appoint a new messenger in the first one's presence.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who rules on the case and defends his ruling.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: Quoted by the Sages, citing his father Rav Huna in the name of Rav.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Father of Rabba bar Rav Huna, quoted in the name of Rav.

people.name: Rav
people.about: An earlier Sage whose ruling is cited against Rava.

terms.meaning: Formally engaged under Jewish law, which is already legally binding, though the couple do not yet live together.
Calmed and reconciled; the worry is that the husband made up with his wife and cancelled the divorce.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses and quotes.

19.note: A man left a bill of divorce with messengers and said: if I do not arrive within thirty days, let this be a divorce. He came back at the end of the thirtieth day, but the ferry was on the other side of the river and he could not cross. He called to the people across the river, 'See that I have arrived, see that I have arrived!' Shmuel said that does not count as arriving, so the divorce takes effect.
19.why: The discussion is about conditional divorces and circumstances outside a person's control. The next case, about a husband who could not appease his wife, is explained by whether such circumstances count in divorce law.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who rules that calling across the river is not arriving.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end a marriage. Here it was set to take effect only if he failed to return in time.

20.note: A man left a bill of divorce with messengers and said: if I do not make peace with my wife within thirty days, let this be a divorce. He went to appease her, but she would not be appeased. Rav Yosef said: did he give her a basket full of dinars and still she was not appeased? In this version, he had not truly met his own condition, so the divorce takes effect.
20.why: The Gemara gives a second version of Rav Yosef's ruling in which the divorce does not take effect, and explains the two as a dispute over whether circumstances beyond a person's control count in divorce law.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who rules on the case.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end a marriage. Here it was set to take effect only if he failed to make peace with her.
A silver coin.
